pages.title: WHY DID I CHOOSE THIS MAJOR?

children.text:
In our first week, the teacher asked us, “Why did you choose this major?”

I realised I didn’t have a clear answer. I’ve always been interested in design, but I didn’t know much about its social side. To be honest, I kind of ended up in Human-Centred Design without really knowing what to expect.

After our first few classes, I started to see that design wasn’t just about making things. It was also about understanding people, something I still knew very little about. I couldn’t answer the teacher’s question yet, so I decided to keep it in mind as the semester went on.

sections.name: WEEK 01 / My first understanding of disability

children.text: MY FIRST UNDERSTANDING OF DISABILITY

Before these classes, I mainly thought disability was about physical conditions. I knew very little about autism and other disabilities that are not always visible. Learning about different needs made me realise how much I didn’t know. I was only at the beginning of understanding people and their experiences.
✳ STILL FIGURING IT OUT.

pages.title: I WANT TO BE INDEPENDENT. BUT…

children.text: ← BACK TO SELF REFLECTION

sections.name: What the simulation made me notice

children.text:
Through a short classroom experience of navigating without sight and using a wheelchair, I realised how different everyday tasks can feel. It wasn’t the same as living with a disability, but it made me notice things I’d never thought much about.

I noticed something unexpected: I didn’t want people to pay too much attention to me or treat me differently. But when I really needed help, I hoped someone would notice.
I DON’T WANT

Too much attention.
Being treated differently.
BUT I NEED
Help when I actually need it.

This also made me think about helping others. Should I offer help immediately, or wait until someone asks? I realised that helping isn’t only about doing things for another person. It should also respect their independence and give them a choice.

I don’t think being independent means never needing support. What matters is being able to decide when and how to receive it.
MY QUESTION →
What does appropriate help look like?

pages.title: ATTENTION IS NOT ALWAYS CARE.
pages.intro: A moment that changed how I think about observing people.

children.text: 01 / LOOKING BEYOND BEHAVIOUR

I once met an autistic child and thought she was just ‘living in her own world.’ At the time, I didn’t understand much about autism. After learning more and listening to autistic people, I realised that was only my assumption. What I see from the outside doesn’t tell me everything someone is experiencing.
02 / A MOMENT THAT MADE ME THINK

During our project, I saw a father and his autistic son on the MRT. The train was noisy, and the son was covering his ears. I took a photo because I thought it could be useful for my learning. Later, his father came over and asked me to delete it. I realised I had been thinking about my research more than their privacy.
03 / MY REFLECTION

I wanted to understand their experience, but I hadn’t thought enough about how being watched or photographed might feel to them. Good intentions don’t automatically make something respectful. Sometimes, giving people space is more important than getting a closer look.

sections.name: 04 / MY VIEW OF WHEELCHAIR USERS HAS CHANGED

children.text: 04 / MY VIEW HAS CHANGED

Before this project, I hadn’t really thought about how much extra effort some wheelchair users need just to travel. But they are part of the same public space as everyone else. I don’t think we should see them as weak or only feel sorry for them. I respect how they continue going out and living their lives, even when getting around can be difficult.

I also realised that, before I started paying attention to accessibility, I might have been one of the people making things harder for them without noticing. I didn’t think much about standing in a wheelchair space or using an accessible lift. Now, when I take the MRT, I check whether I’m blocking a wheelchair area, and I try to leave those spaces free. If I can use the escalator, I usually choose it instead of the accessible lift.

These may seem like small changes, but this project made me realise that my everyday habits can affect someone else’s independence.
A THOUGHT TO CARRY FORWARD
Sometimes, respect means knowing when not to look.

pages.title: IS HAVING ACCESS ENOUGH?
pages.intro: Starting to question what accessibility really means.

children.text: 01 / WHAT I USED TO THINK
I used to think that having lifts, ramps and wheelchair spaces was enough to make a place accessible. I didn’t pay much attention to how people actually reached or used them.
02 / WHAT CHANGED

As we discussed wheelchair users’ experiences, I started asking different questions. What if a lift is hard to find? What if the route is much longer? What if someone has to ask for help each time they travel?
03 / MY THOUGHT

I realised that design should not only provide a facility. It should also make it possible for people to use it with less difficulty and more independence. There was still a lot we needed to find out from real users.
MY REFLECTION
Accessible on paper does not always mean easy in real life.

pages.title: BUILDING THE FOUNDATION.
pages.intro: Learning not to fall in love with the first design idea.

sections.name: 01 / A WAY I THINK ABOUT DESIGN

children.text: 01 / A WAY I THINK ABOUT DESIGN
Design feels a bit like building a house. Before making something beautiful, we need a good foundation. For us, that foundation was understanding the problem and the people affected by it.

sections.name: 02 / AN IDEA IS ONLY A START

children.text: 02 / AN IDEA IS ONLY A START
It was exciting to come up with ways to improve the wheelchair space on the MRT. But I also started wondering whether what looked helpful to us would feel the same to wheelchair users.
03 / MY QUESTION

I learned that our first idea is only our starting point. We still have to listen to users and be willing to change it. I want our design to make their journey easier, not tell them how they should behave.
MY REFLECTION
A design is not finished just because we have an idea.

pages.title: WHEN AN IDEA MEETS REAL LIFE.
pages.intro: This week taught me as much about teamwork as it did about design.

sections.name: 01 / A WAY I THINK ABOUT DESIGN

children.text: 01 / WHEN DESIGN MEETS REAL USERS

This week I learned that an idea can seem perfect in a designer’s mind. But when we actually show it to users, we start to notice many small problems we didn’t expect. We have to keep testing, listening and making changes. A good design should work for the people using it, rather than making them change the way they do things just to fit our design.

sections.name: 02 / AN IDEA IS ONLY A START

children.text: 02 / ACCESSIBILITY IS MORE THAN FACILITIES

The government can provide accessible facilities to support people who need them. But how useful these spaces are also depends on how everyone uses them in daily life. For example, having a wheelchair area means little if other passengers keep standing in it. I started to realise that accessibility is not just about putting a facility there. It also depends on how we share and respect public spaces.
03 / LEARNING TO WORK AS A TEAM

I learned a lot from working with different people in my group. I saw their strengths and also the things we could improve. It also made me notice my own weaknesses. I know I need to take action more quickly and be more careful and organised with my work. Sometimes I don’t think the assignment itself is that difficult. The harder part is getting everyone’s different ideas to move in the same direction. That takes a lot of communication, listening and understanding.
WHAT I WANT TO REMEMBER
We should design for people to use, not ask people to change for our design.

pages.title: CAN WE FEEL COLOUR WITHOUT SEEING IT?
pages.intro: A question about losing sight, the smell of rain, and how I began to think differently about colour.

sections.name: 01 / A WAY I THINK ABOUT DESIGN

children.text: 01 / THE SENSE I WOULD BE MOST AFRAID TO LOSE

After doing so much research, I started asking myself: if I had to lose one of my senses, which one would I be most afraid of losing? For me, it would be sight. I honestly cannot imagine a life without seeing sunlight, nature and all the colours around me. How would I experience those things if I could no longer see them? This question stayed in my mind.

sections.name: 02 / AN IDEA IS ONLY A START

children.text: 02 / THINKING ABOUT OTHER SENSES

Through our interviews, I learned that some people with visual impairment use sounds, touch and smells in ways I had never paid much attention to. I started wondering whether these senses could help someone experience the things I usually understand through sight, especially nature and colour.
03 / AN IDEA AFTER THE RAIN

One day, I was walking along a street in Singapore after the rain. I could smell pandan and fresh grass in the air. It made me think of the colour green, even before I really looked around. Suddenly I wondered: if someone cannot see a colour, could a familiar smell help them feel or imagine it in their own way?

Of course, smell cannot replace sight. But maybe it could offer another way to connect with nature. That was where my first idea for a sensory exhibition began.
A QUESTION TO TAKE FORWARD
If we cannot see a colour, can we experience it in another way?

pages.title: CAN WE FEEL THE SEASONS?
pages.intro: The Feeling Garden — a four-season sensory exhibition inspired by life in Singapore.

children.text: 01 / WHY I CHOSE THIS IDEA

Singapore doesn’t really have four distinct seasons. That made me wonder: what would spring, summer, autumn and winter feel like if we couldn’t see them? I also noticed how a familiar perfume can bring back a memory or a feeling. That connection between smell, memory and emotion became the starting point for my exhibition.
02 / DESIGNING BEYOND SIGHT

I designed four areas using different flowers, scents, sounds and temperatures: peach blossom for spring, lotus for summer, osmanthus for autumn and wintersweet for winter. I planned an open looping route with tactile guidance, so visitors could move through the seasons in a clear order. I wanted people with visual impairment to explore more independently, but I didn’t want the exhibition to be only for them.

sections.name: 03 / WHAT THIS MADE ME THINK ABOUT

children.text: 03 / WHAT THIS MADE ME THINK ABOUT

This project made me realise that a space doesn’t always need to be understood through sight. Smell, touch and sound can tell their own stories. But designing a route that I think is easy to follow doesn’t mean it will work for someone who is blind. I would still need to ask real visitors and learn how they experience the space.

sections.name: 04 / A Designer Is a Bridge / The Answer I Was Looking For

children.text: 04 / I THINK I FOUND MY ANSWER

At the beginning of the semester, I couldn’t really answer why I chose this major. After doing more research and working on these projects, I think I’m starting to find my answer.

I want to make designs that feel warm and human, not just things that look good. Sometimes I feel like our role is to be a bridge between the people who use a design and the ideas we create. We need to listen to what people actually need, and turn that into something they can really use in everyday life. Otherwise, even a beautiful design might not mean much.

I also feel that the design we do should have warmth. It is not just about showing our own ideas. As we design, we keep learning from the people who will actually use our work. Sometimes I feel like a social designer needs to be a bit of an all-rounder. We have to observe, listen, communicate, research, test and keep improving. I still have a lot to learn, but that is what makes this kind of design meaningful to me.

This also brought me back to what I said at the beginning of the semester. I love listening to different people’s stories because everyone has their own story to tell. Through their experiences, I get to see a bigger world and learn things I might never have discovered on my own. Maybe this is what drew me to this course in the first place.
PROJECT PRESENTATION · 8 SLIDES
VIEW ORIGINAL PRESENTATION ↗

sections.name: A question I want to carry forward

children.text: WHAT I WANT TO REMEMBER ✳
Good design isn’t only about what we create. It should work for the people who use it.

pages.title: SENSESA — WORLD BEYOND SIGHT
pages.intro: An Inclusive Sensory Community Centre · Text-based version of the original 8-page presentation.

children.text: 01 / THE FEELING GARDEN
A sensory exhibition for people with and without sight. Inspired by the changing seasons, it invites visitors to experience nature in a different way.
02 / PERSONAL EXPERIENCE

Different scents remind me of different moments in my life. Sometimes a perfume brings back a picture, an emotion or a feeling.

Smell → Memory → Emotion
03 / FROM SCENT TO SEASONS

In Singapore, we don’t really experience four distinct seasons. Instead of only hearing about them through news or weather forecasts, what if we let nature tell us what each season smells like?

Spring — Peach blossom
Summer — Lotus
Autumn — Osmanthus
Winter — Wintersweet
04 / COMMUNITY CONCEPT

My main target group is people born blind, but I don’t want the space to be only for them. I want everyone to explore the four seasons through smell, touch and sound.

Traditional museum: Look → Understand
Sensory museum: Smell · Touch · Hear → Experience
05 / A GUIDED SENSORY JOURNEY

The exhibition follows Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter. Central exhibits offer things to smell, touch and hear. A tactile guided path supports more independent navigation, and a shared area lets visitors relax and connect with others.
06 / FOUR SEASONS, FOUR FEELINGS

SPRING — Peach blossom scents, birdsong and a gentle breeze.

SUMMER — Lotus scents, warm air and flowing water.

AUTUMN — Osmanthus fragrance, falling leaves and the sound of wind.

WINTER — Wintersweet, cool air and a quiet atmosphere.

Visitors can touch artificial flowers and explore at their own pace.
07 / OUR DESIGN GOAL
To create a museum experience that people can explore with or without sight, in an open looping space that welcomes different ways of experiencing nature.
08 / THANK YOU

THE FEELING GARDEN

A sensory journey beyond sight.

pages.title: FROM CONFUSION TO A SHARED MAP.
pages.intro: Starting our wayfinding project, working together and finding a common design style.

sections.name: 01 / A WAY I THINK ABOUT DESIGN

children.text: 01 / NOT KNOWING WHERE TO START
When we first started the wayfinding project, I honestly had no idea where to begin. Everything felt a bit confusing, and I couldn’t really picture what our map should look like.

sections.name: 02 / AN IDEA IS ONLY A START

children.text: 02 / FINDING INSPIRATION TOGETHER
But once we started discussing ideas as a group, looking for inspiration and going out to investigate the route, things began to take shape. Before long, we had our first rough map.
03 / TURNING OUR IDEAS INTO DIGITAL MAPS

The next challenge was putting our ideas onto the computer. Everyone had a different design style, so it was difficult to make a whole set of maps that looked like they belonged together. Luckily, everyone in our group was easy to communicate with and open to different opinions. We talked things through, made adjustments and managed to move the project forward quite quickly.

sections.name: 04 / MY ROLE IN THE GROUP — A BRICK WHERE NEEDED

children.text: 04 / FINDING MY PLACE IN THE TEAM

I also realised that I don’t think I’m very suited to being the leader of a group. I worry too much about what everyone thinks, and sometimes that makes it hard for me to make a decision. I want everyone to feel comfortable, but that’s actually quite difficult.

So I chose to follow the team’s lead and help wherever I was needed. I like to joke that I’m a brick — just move me wherever you need me! 😆
WHAT HELPED US MOVE FORWARD
Good communication and being open to each other’s ideas.

pages.title: MAPS, MAPS, EVERYWHERE.
pages.intro: A week of collecting ideas, organising everything and drawing maps nonstop.

children.text: 01 / DRAWING MAPS ALL THE TIME
This week felt like I was constantly collecting ideas, sorting things out and turning them into maps. I was drawing so much that it felt like I could still see maps when I closed my eyes! 😅
02 / LOOKING BACK
At the time, I was honestly quite tired. But now, looking back at everything we made, I actually feel pretty proud of it.

pages.title: MAKING THE PIECES FIT.
pages.intro: Different ideas, one map, and some small changes that matter.

children.text: 01 / PUTTING DIFFERENT IDEAS TOGETHER
At first, everyone’s maps looked like separate pieces. Combining them was actually harder than I expected. We had to keep adjusting the colours and layouts until they felt like one set.
02 / SMALL CHANGES CAN MATTER

The video was another example. Changing the view from a standing guide to a wheelchair user’s and a caregiver’s perspective felt closer to the people we’re designing for. Sometimes a small change can make a design feel much more inclusive.

pages.title: MY MIND IS ALREADY ON THE SKI SLOPES.
pages.intro: YN’s little class games, discovering something about myself, and my very disciplined classmates.

children.text: 01 / LEARNING THROUGH LITTLE GAMES

YN’s classes are always so much fun. The little games help me get to know myself and my classmates without making things feel awkward or too personal. They bring people closer together, and I think I could use them in future interviews or even at work. I also found out that my working memory is much worse than I thought, haha!
02 / EVERYONE IS SO DISCIPLINED…

This week’s activity made me realise how healthy, disciplined and hardworking everyone in my group is. Meanwhile, my mind is already halfway to the snowy mountains! Hmm… maybe one day I’ll fall in love with reading too. 😆

pages.title: 50 OUT OF 100, BUT STILL MOVING FORWARD.
pages.intro: Looking back on this semester, finding my place in a team, and what social design means to me.

children.text: 01 / LOOKING BACK AT THIS SEMESTER

Looking back at this whole semester, I actually gained a lot. At first I was excited to take on new challenges. But after joining a group, I sometimes felt lost about where I fitted in. I wasn’t always good at managing my emotions either, especially around people close to me. Luckily, we got through it, and our ideas slowly started to become something real.
02 / MAYBE 50 OUT OF 100

If I had to grade myself this semester, I’d give myself 50 out of 100. I don’t think I contributed as much as some of my teammates. I really wanted to learn and help, but when I noticed my skills and English weren’t as good as theirs, I secretly felt sad sometimes. So I tried to do what I could: finish my tasks on time and not slow everyone down. The sun will still rise tomorrow, right? I’ll sort out my feelings and keep going!
03 / WHAT DOES SOCIAL FUTURES MEAN?

I used to wonder what “Social Futures” actually means. After this semester, I feel like understanding people is already a huge subject. How do we help people and design communicate with each other? Maybe that’s part of the answer. Seeing our project slowly turn into something real gives me more satisfaction than a drawing I spent a whole day making.
04 / MY DESIGN ETHOS — WITH PEOPLE

My ETHOS is quite simple: I believe good design should have warmth and feelings. It should be created with people, not just for them. I like listening to other people’s stories and learning about worlds different from my own. Social design isn’t one person’s idea — people from different communities make it together. I like that we can bring some warmth to users, and they can bring warmth to us too. That’s why I really enjoy this kind of design.

sections.name: 05 / CAN THIS DESIGN PAY MY BILLS?

children.text: 05 / CAN THIS DESIGN PAY MY BILLS?

But I still have one very simple question: can I actually make a living doing this kind of design after graduation? Haha, maybe I’ll answer that when I graduate! For now, I’ll enjoy the process and respect the result.
